projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Stanley Resnick was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Today is Sunday, January 12th, 2003, and this is the beginning of an interview with Stanley Resnick at my home, 808 Oak Lawn Avenue in Winston Salem, North Carolina. Retired Lieutenant Colonel Stanley Resnick is 83 years old, having been born on October 8th, 1919, in New York City. We're going to begin the interview now with my father.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Dad, can you tell us when you decided or -- to join the service, and how old you were, and what year that was, and where you were?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: I always had an intense desire to be a part of the United States Air Force. I had -- I intended initially to enter the cadet program but was sidetracked, you might say, because of the inability to completely pass a physical examination for entry purposes. As a result, in the summer of 1940, exactly the month of September, I took the advice of an officer at Selfridge Air Force Base, and he suggested that I enlist in the United States Air Force at Chanute Field, Rantoul, Illinois. For the edification of all, Rantoul is 114 miles south of Chicago. I entered -- I took the advice of this officer, and on September 23rd, 1940, I boarded a bus for Rantoul, Illinois. I arrived there at midnight and was escorted to the recruit detachment at Chanute Field. Chanute Field, for intents and purposes, is the Air Force military training course for people who intend to work on aircraft. It is a course approximately 22 weeks long. And it was a good idea that I go down there, learn to relax somewhat, and eventually was able to pass a physical examination. However, I did complete the entire 22-week course and became a full-fledged flight engineer on the aircraft that was located at Barksdale Field, Louisiana. Barksdale Field was my first assignment upon graduating from the school at Chanute Field.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Okay. When you first got into the service, was there any type of boot camp or physical training that you had to go through, or was it just the training course that you talked about?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: When we arrived there, we did go through, you might say, some recruit training, marching, how to -- learn how to take care of yourself so far as handling bedding equipment, things like that. We were taught to do that. And approximately -- That took approximately three weeks. And then we were -- Then we entered the actual training program for -- for flight engineers.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And what rank were you?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: I was a private.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: A private?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Private. Private.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And then how long did you serve in that capacity?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: I served in that capacity for approximately one and one-half years.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Okay. And then you went to officers candidate school, was it?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Yes. I -- after arriving -- serving on the flight line at Barksdale Air Force Base, Louisiana, I eventually was capable of passing the physical examination and was sent to -- to training at Montgomery, Alabama, known as Maxwell Field. That was the centralized location for all incoming cadets. And we spent a very short time there firing the pistols, marching, physically training, and was eventually assigned to the navigation school at Mather Air Force Base, Sacramento, California. And that was in the month of February, 1942. We embarked from Maxwell Field to -- to Mather Field. The course at Mather Field for Air Force navigators was exactly 15 weeks long. We spent 15 weeks learning how to direct aircraft from place to place, and after graduating we were -- from that course in June 13th, 1942, I was assigned to my first combat organization in Columbia, South Carolina. That assignment lasted, strangely enough, only one day. We were sent to the organization known as the 12th Bomb Group at -- in central -- north central Louisiana. And there we were finally placed into organizations and assigned with the people who you were going to fly with actually in combat.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And when did you get your assignment that you were going to go to North Africa?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: We got our assignment to go to North Africa in August of 1942. Prior to that, though, we were awaiting our aircraft, and at the same time did some training in -- some simulated combat training at Esler Field, Louisiana. That's where the organization originally formed known as the 12th Bomb Group. The 12th Bomb Group was composed of four individual squadrons: the 81st squadron, the 82nd, the 83rd, and, strangely enough, the 434, which was an organization that was formed from an organization in north -- in Seattle, Washington. It was there that the 434th organization was formed and was inserted into the 12th Bomb Group as the fourth squadron, and that was the squadron I was assigned to, 434.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Okay. Can you tell us about your trip from the United States over to North Africa, what route you took and what the process was?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: After we got our assignment to go to the Middle East, we boarded our aircraft, and our first stop, you might say, was for the purpose of getting equipment, finding out the actual route that you were going to take over, fly to -- a training mission, and just getting associated with the airplane, the people you were going to fly with. And after that, we finally were sent -- given the word to go. The organization left in four squadrons. The 81st left first, 82nd, 83rd, and, strangely enough, my organization was the last to depart from Esler Field, Louisiana. We arrived at Morrison Field, West Palm Beach, Florida, and that's where we got our equipment and our briefing on the route that we were going to fly. We were there approximately ten days, and finally we were given the word to go. As I mentioned, we were the last organization to leave. The first part of the overall destination to North Africa, to Egypt, was Puerto Rico. We flew from West Palm Beach to the first stop at Ramey Field, Puerto Rico, in -- wherever you might want to call that location. From Puerto Rico, our next assignment -- we stayed overnight, incidentally. Our next point en route was Trinidad and -- in the Caribbean. We stayed in Trinidad one night, and from there our next assignment -- our next destination was Belém, Brazil. Belém, Brazil was located close on the north -- north part of South America, and we made the over-water flight from Trinidad to Belém. En route -- The route took us exactly -- beam off Devil's Island. We used Devil's Island as a point to determine our speed, because our turn into Belém, into the Amazon River, was over water. So that gave us a very accurate ground speed, at which time we turned south down the Amazon to Belém. Belém, Brazil is one of the larger towns in the country of Brazil. It's very, very well known. We stayed at Belém, Brazil approximately four days, and from there our next assignment -- our next route was Natal, Brazil. Natal, Brazil was the northeast part of the country and right on the coast line of South America. There we spent, again, approximately four days getting our planes, you might say, corrected for any malfunctions or anything that needed attention. Now from there, it was -- the next assignment, the next route, the destination was an island -- was a small island in the Atlantic known as Ascension Island. Ascension Island was about 1500 miles from the coast -- from the coast of Natal, and there it was sort of a dangerous flight, because it was flown in the daytime. There was no stars to orient yourself. At any rate, there was -- I like to mention a very powerful radio station that existed at Ascension Island, so powerful we were able to pick it up from Natal, Brazil, from the airfield at Natal. And, fortunately, that device was available for us, and we just followed that radio beam straight in, and it was very easy to locate Ascension Island. Ascension Island had a characteristic cloud cover, and it happened that way every day. And there we stayed approximately two days, got off, straightened out, and there -- that was the departure point for, finally, the country of Africa. We made that flight entering the southwest part of -- you might say, of Africa. And the name of the place was the Gold Coast, Accra in the Gold Coast. And that's where we finally, you might say, embraced the country of Africa. And there we stayed approximately four days, and we met some of the people who had been in the desert fighting the German North Africa Corps, and they gave us some information, not very encouraging, because we found out how -- what a formidable foe the Germans -- the German people were, particularly at the _______ Africa Corps. And we were sort of discouraged a bit, but nevertheless we had an assignment, and we were on our way. Now, we went through quite a bit of Africa before we finally hit our destination. Upon leaving Accra, our first stop was Lagos, and that was in Nigeria. It was -- We didn't actually land there. It was a turning point for our next -- for our next destination, Kano, Nigeria. And there, that's where we -- we entered into some pretty rough terrain and were fortunate enough to be able to land there without any serious problem. Kano, Nigeria was our stop, and we stayed there approximately two days and managed to meet some of the natives there, and they did -- they were kind enough to do our laundry for us, and they were very accommodating. Our next stop from Kano, Nigeria was in French Equatorial Africa. ________ was the name of the town in there, and that was hardly anything to worth mentioning. It was just plain desert, you might say, and the food there was very -- very poor. But nevertheless, it was a stop. From there our next place was -- our next departure or destination, I should say, was in the Anglo Egyptian Sudan, _______ in the Anglo Egyptian Sudan. However, en route to there, our route took us over a place known as Lake Chad, and Lake Chad was a part of French Equatorial Africa and was a place that for some reason or another a German airplane managed to find its way in there, and they just created an awful lot of damage on the ground. As a result, any airplanes flying over that area -- Lake Chad was actually -- the name of it was Fort Lamy, L-a-m-y. And we were ordered, when we arrived at that point, to make three complete 360-degree turns to the left as a means of identifying ourselves, which we did, and finally it took our ________ into the Sudan. The Sudan -- _______ was the largest city in that area. And there we spent, again, approximately four days, and we were able to do a little bit of shopping in the area, because there were some stores. It was a reasonably large town. Now, we were on our last route, the last, you might say, flight, the flight course to our final destination of Ismailia, Egypt, but before going to Ismailia, Egypt, we flew straight due north following the Nile River, one of the largest rivers in the world, and we flew up to about 100 miles south of Cairo. When we arrived at that point, we made a turn to the east to another roughly 100 miles to our final destination of -- in Egypt. It was an RAF station, RAF Ismailia. And the RAF people were in charge, and we were simply tenants there. And it was there that we stayed a considerable length of time, because we had a lot of training to do. We had to be familiar with a very strange terrain. And, strangely enough, when we arrived there, as I mentioned, we were the final squadron to reach that point. We found out that four -- that the four aircraft were actually shot down, of our organization. Now, this -- I should -- this is of considerable significance. If you recall, I mentioned there were four squadrons in the 12th Bomb Group. The 81st and the 82nd were assigned to Ismailia, and the other two organizations -- hold on. Excuse me. The 81st and the 82nd was assigned to an organization south -- in the south part of the Suez Canal known as ________, and the 83rd and the 434 was assigned to Ismailia. So, effectively, for a considerable length of time, the 12th Bomb Group actually operated as two separate organizations, and we stayed that way for a good while as we proceeded westward against the German Africa Corps. As we moved, we moved as two separate organizations. Now, the B25s, as we received them, did not have what we call anything to dampen the flame of the engine. The engine produced a noticeable flame, a light at night, and when you fly at night, the German night fighters -- we were easy prey for the German night fighters, and four of our aircraft were shot down. And that was in the first -- of the organizations of _______. And for a good while, we didn't do any night flying, because we had to have flame dampeners installed on the engines. And that is where we stayed for a considerable length of time until we started our move, our formal move, against the African Corps.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: So how many missions did you fly in North Africa?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Between North Africa and Sicily, I flew 58 missions.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Fifty-eight missions?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Were there many casualties in your unit?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Yes, there were several casualties. And one of the aircraft that was shot down was our wing commander, our group commander, Colonel Charles Goodrich. Colonel Goodrich was a man who was a West Pointer and a very severe, you might say, type of person. He was a person who people held a lot of respect for and never attempted to cross his path. But he was one of the first aircraft of the four that was shot down.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And do you know what became of him?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Yes. He was injured very seriously. He was a prisoner of war. He was on the Island of Crete for practically the entire war and was eventually returned to the States.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: I see. And do you remember any of these missions that you flew particularly well, or any of them that were especially memorable to you?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Actually, strangely enough, one of the first missions was the first night mission over the German airfield in Egypt. And the Germans were very good with their search lights, and as we came over this first target where the search lights -- the lights came up, we dropped our bombs and got out of there in a hurry, because the German night fighters were also lurking around.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: But the German -- the -- The flight of a really serious nature was eventually -- when we started off our big push on October 24th against the German -- against the Africa Corps, the _______ organization, and they were very good with radar control antiaircraft. They had a special device known as -- It was the 88-millimeter. The 88-millimeter was a dual-purpose gun, because it was used for fighting on the ground, or ground fighting, and also it was able to fly as antiaircraft. It was dual-purpose and very accurate. And we got hit pretty badly. We didn't lose very many aircraft, but our aircraft was damaged with the accuracy of the 88-millimeter. That was a very famous shooting device.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: So you were responsible for the navigation for your flight over to Africa and then all the bombing missions that you flew?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: You see, the B25, while it had a place for a navigator and a radar -- and a bombardier, the missions were so short in length that it was not really necessary to have a navigator in the aircraft. The bombardier could do his own navigation, because it was such short distances that we flew, you see, to catch up to where the Germans were. However, eventually, the navigators received sufficient training in using the special bomb sight that we had, and sooner or later the bombardiers were able to fly by themselves, the navigators were able to fly by themselves and do their own navigation and their own bombing. So that's the way things were for a good part of the flight. It wasn't necessary to have a navigator and a bombardier inside each aircraft.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: When did you leave North Africa to go to Sicily?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: We left there -- Well, I was overseas a total of 13 months -- approximately ten months. I was on Crete for three months before we departed in September. So September, I was about -- in June, I would say, of 1942, we left North Africa for Sicily.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And what was the reason that you left? Was there some conclusion to your --

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Because we occupied Sicily. That was the purpose.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: But had you pushed Rommel's troops back in North Africa?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: The war was over in April of 1942. The Africa Corps surrendered.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Rommel went back to Germany, received the orders of Adolf Hitler, and that was the end of that. That was the end of the North African campaign, was in, roughly, June of 1942.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: So what were you doing in Sicily, then?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: We were bombing Sicily. We bombed Sicily from North Africa and also when we occupied it.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Okay. And who were you bombing on Sicily?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: The Germans.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Okay. And that wasn't Rommel's group?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: No, that was an entirely different group.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Okay. And then when you left Sicily, did you return to the United States?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Returned to the United States. September of '40.... (PAUSE.) MR. BRUCE RESNICK: I was asking what was life like when you weren't flying on a mission. What did you do during the day? Was there any type of entertainment? How did you occupy yourself? Those types of things.

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Well, during the day we were able to play volleyball, we played softball. We had teams among the people in the organization. And sometimes we managed to obtain a Jeep and drive to some of the nearby towns, for example, the city of Tunis. I was sent there because I had some knowledge of French and was able to talk to the people, to a certain extent. And we purchased what you call wine, liquors of various kind, there. And we spent time doing things like that. We were able to get away from the field, so to speak. Actually, the field was nothing more than just plain desert which was smoothed out with our heavy-duty equipment, and that's what we had for airfields all the way through North Africa and into Sicily.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Was it on one of these trips that you went to the pyramids in Cairo?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: That was way back. We went to the pyramids in Cairo from our original station in Ismailia. We were able to get into the town of Cairo, got -- managed also to obtain rooms in the famous hotels, the hotel that was available there, and then we actually drove to where the pyramids were and the sphinx. And we sat on camels. We have a picture taken of our entire crew on camels.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Was Cairo a neutral city? I thought you told me at one time that you saw German officers walking around.

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: That was in Algiers.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: In Algiers. And what was that occasion there? Why were you there and --

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: At that point -- We made various trips to Algiers from our station in North Africa. That was -- I would say from the last airfield that we occupied in North Africa, we made various trips to Algiers and stayed overnight there, you know, just sort of like you were on leave, so to speak.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: So who occupied that city?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: It was -- There was no German people there. It was just the French.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: So what was this German officer doing that you saw?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: He was a prisoner.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: He was a prisoner, I see. Okay. Okay. And I think you told me at one time that a plane, a German plane, had been shot down, and someone wanted to take the joystick from it. What was that occasion?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: That was during the time we were still in Libya, and what we did, it was -- Part of our assignment was to transport bombs, actually transport bombs to the -- to our aircraft. As we were doing that, there was a lot of shot-down -- a lot of enemy aircraft that had been shot down in the desert, Italian aircraft and German aircraft. And this one particular registered 109 happened to be available, and to do anything about it, about the _______ 109, the way the German people designed their aircraft, the control stick was a thing of beauty; and, personally, I would liked to have had that as a trophy, but I was afraid because the Germans were known for booby traps -- booby-trapping aircraft. Nevertheless, one sergeant managed to get -- attained enough nerve to get in there, and he took that control stick completely out of the aircraft. That was in the early part of the war.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: So were your supplies good while you were in camp? Did you have enough food to eat, and things like that?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: We were on British rations most of the time.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: What was a typical meal like?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Spam.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Spam. I see.

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Ate more Spam than you could possibly have.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: So was your weight -- Did you lose a lot of weight when you were gone?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: I lost a considerable amount of weight during the entire time I was in the Middle East.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: I see. And were you able to take showers and things of that nature? How did people keep clean?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: If we took two showers during the whole time we were there, that was -- that was while we were in the desert -- that was saying a lot. It just was not available. If you go into Algiers or places that was hotels, yes. Or Cairo or Alexandria, Egypt. We -- Some of those big hotel resorts, you were able to have -- attain the living you were accustomed to at one time.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: How did you shave in the morning, and things like that?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: With cold water.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Cold water. Okay. And when you left Sicily, did you turn in any of your supplies? How did things work? Did you have to turn things in?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: I turned in a jacket, which I wished I hadn't have done.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Was that your bombing jacket?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: It was a bombing jacket. The reason why I did that is because I knew I would be able to obtain another one when I arrived back in the States, through our supplies, but it wasn't as good an item as the one I had when I originally went overseas. Other than that, we just left anything that was -- that the fellows could use while we were there.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: So they didn't bring their own equipment over, I mean, their own jackets and supplies and things? You got those once you got there?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: We brought our own.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Okay. So you brought your jacket over with you, but you left it there in case somebody needed it?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Coolest thing to do.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Well, when you returned home, what month and year was that?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: September of 1943.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: September of '43. And where were you stationed then?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: We were sent -- We were permitted to go to our own homes where we lived, and we stayed there approximately a month waiting for assignments, you see. When we finally got our assignment, it was to a rest-and-recuperation place. It happened to be Atlantic City, New Jersey. And we stayed there 30 days before we finally got our assignment, and we lived like kings.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: I see. And what was your next assignment?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: My first assignment was MacDill Field, Florida, a B17 training station, and I instructed new crews coming in that were getting ready to go over to England to the 8th Air Force.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: I wasn't there very long, because the B29 came into view, and it was an airplane that far superseded the B17. It was a plane that was to be used against the Japanese in the Pacific.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: So the war was not over at that point. So were you preparing to go on additional missions?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: I was preparing to go to the Pacific, and I managed to go -- Well, in order to qualify for the B29, you had to be a navigator and a bombardier. I already was a navigator, and I managed to obtain the opportunity to go to bombardier school. In addition to going to bombardier school, I went to gunnery school to fire machine guns, and there -- and was assigned finally to an organization called B29 training to eventually go to -- well, first, Guam. But I wasn't in that organization very long, because I had the misfortune of having a ruptured appendix, and they wouldn't allow me to stay in that organization. It was a long story of being able to try and stay with that organization, but that ruptured appendix, they refused to let me do that. So through what you call a lot of help on the outside, I managed to go to the headquarters and -- where our -- that was in the States, that was assigned to the B29 program, and I explained the problem, that I wanted to go overseas in the worst way. And, fortunately, I was able to be given another B29 assignment, and we went through the entire program of training. We received our aircraft. We were going to Okinawa, was our assignment. When we were at Kearney, Nebraska, which was our staging area, like our departure point for the Pacific, two atomic bombs were dropped. And that, of course, stopped the war right then and there, and I never was able to get a second tour to -- on the B29s.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: In terms of training, was the navigational school longer or was the bombardier school longer, about the same?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Approximately the same. About 15 weeks apiece.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And how about the gunnery school, how long was that?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Six weeks.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Six weeks, I see. When the war was over, what did you do at that point?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: When the war was over, we wondered what was going to happen to us, because there was rumors of being -- of people being released from the service. However, there was a program known as the sunset program for the purpose of flying B29s from Guam that were stationed over there while the war was still going on, and returning them to the States, and they used some of the people who had B29 experience. And they formed combat crews, and they flew us over to Guam, and we -- from there we were assigned planes, and we flew from Guam back to the organization in the States that housed these B29s that we returned.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: So you were ferrying these planes back?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: I was ferrying them back.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And how many of these trips did you make?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Three.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Three. And at some point they released people from the service?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And when was that that you were released?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: In the fall of '46.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: 1946. And you were married at that time; is that correct?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And you had been married about how long when you got released?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: From August --

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: About a year or so.

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: No, no. Months.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Just months. Okay. '46, okay. I see. And then you were -- had a civilian job for a short period of time?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Yes. We purchased an ice cream organization -- bar and light lunches.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And how long did you own that?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Eleven months.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And how did you decide that you wanted to get back in the service?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: I just wanted to get back.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: How did you go about doing that?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: I went to the Pentagon Building in Washington.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And who did you talk to there?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: The people who assigned the people. Told them what had happened, that I should not have been released at the time. It was very unfortunate that I was in a bad position. I was in an organization that had no real serious assignment in the Air Force at that time.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And was there any particular reason that they accepted you back in? Were they preparing for some other campaigns?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: I do not know why -- what it was, but they accepted me.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Okay. And what was your immediate assignment once you got back in?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Spokane, Washington.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And what year was that?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: That was 1948, January of '48.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: I see. And so you stayed in the service for your entire career; is that correct?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Yes, you might say.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And when did you retire from the service?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Retired from the service January of '71.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And at what rank were you?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Lieutenant Colonel.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Okay. And you also served in Korea; is that correct?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Served in Korea, yes.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Could you tell us a little bit about that experience? Where were you during that war?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Yes. We were assigned to a place known as Yokota, 20 miles from the city of Tokyo, and it was there where we flew B29s. We flew our own planes from Spokane over to Japan, and there is where we started our flying serious missions against the North Korean people.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: So you had 58 missions in Europe?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Fifty-six.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And 56 in Korea?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Can you compare the difference between a mission in Korea with one in Africa?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: A mission in Africa was only two hours long.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Short missions. And from there we flew -- our missions were about eight hours long.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: So you flew from Japan to Korea and back?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: And back again.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Did you perceive in your mind one being more dangerous than the other?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: No. No comparison.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: In what sense?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: In Africa and Sicily, it was considerably more dangerous because of the Germans.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: I see. I see. And how long were you in Japan?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Eight months.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Eight months.

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: And we returned to the States in April of '51.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: So you're one of the few people that's a veteran of three wars, World War II, and Korea, and Vietnam. What was your assignment during the Vietnam War? What did you do there?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: I was a squadron commander of an avionics maintenance squadron of F4Cs fighter aircraft. It was the 8th Tact Fighter Wing, and it was our responsibility to monitor the instruments and engines and anything associated with the airplane.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: So you did maintenance on these planes --

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: -- is that correct? And what period of time were you serving in the Vietnam War.

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: The Vietnam -- exactly one year.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And what was the starting date of that?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Starting date was July of '68 to July of '69.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: I see. And then you remained in the service another two years upon your return?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: And your terminal assignment was?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Wright Patterson Air Force Base.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: What did you do there?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Squadron commander of a missile squadron, missiles that were assigned to fly on the B52.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Very good. (END OF FIRST SESSION.) MR. BRUCE RESNICK: We're continuing this interview. This is January 19th, the year 2003. This will conclude the interview after we finish speaking here today.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Dad, we were talking last week about your experiences in World War II, Korea, and the Vietnam War, and you were kind enough to give us your recollections and your experiences. During the war, did you receive any special awards or medals?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: I was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross twice for superior flying; I was awarded the Air Medal with 12 oak leaf clusters, and that is primarily awarded for numbers of missions that are flown. And then for overall distinguished service in all phases of my career, I was awarded the Meritorious Service Medal.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Very good. Thank you. You told us that you had some stories that you'd like to tell from some of your experiences in the service.

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: One sort of humorous incident took place. You might recall that the engines assigned to the B25 did not have flame dampeners, which effectively caused the airplane to light up at night, and it was easy prey for the German night fighters. And we were grounded as a result of -- We were grounded while these flame dampeners were being awarded. Nevertheless, some of our airplanes were available for flying night flying, and the wing commander or rather the group commander insisted that people fly. One of the navigator's name was Monroe P. Force, and, strangely enough, he was a classmate of mine, and he refused to fly, and he told that to the group commander. And the group commander says, "Mister, you're under arrest. Return to your quarters."

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: So did he ever end up flying on the mission, or what happened?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: More strangely, the group commander was shot down very shortly thereafter, and nothing was ever -- nothing ever took place. "Return to his quarters" was rather comical.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: I see. Any other stories that you would like to share?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: This was rather comical. Tom Cunningham, one of the aircraft commanders, seemed to be ill quite a bit during the time we were over there, and he spent a great number of months in the hospital in Cairo. And one evening we -- We'd normally hold a role call. All of a sudden, out of a clear blue sky, Tom Cunningham shows up, and one of the fellows says, "Tom Cunningham. The war is over now!" And he had a very sheepish grin on his face when he came in.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Anything else that you can recall that you want to share?

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: One time when we were at Palestine, right outside of Tel Aviv, one of our pilots who happened to be with me at the time, we were walking around the field, and he spotted an unattended motorcycle. And Bradshaw liked to ride motorcycles, so without asking any permission, without even looking around to see who owned it, he took the motorcycle and just rode around the field. And on it was his navigator, J.P. Wright, riding on the back seat. All of a -- so he was riding around, riding around, and he came to a complete stop, and J.P. Wright slipped off the back seat. And he was stopped. And who was there but this captain who owned the motorcycle. And it was very embarrassing for Bradshaw to tell him that he was just borrowing his motorcycle. That, I thought, was quite interesting.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Very good. Well, it sounds like you had a lot of experiences, some of them amusing.

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: They were.

sp.speaker: Bruce G. Resnick
sp.p: Well, thank you very much. This concludes the interview.

sp.speaker: Stanley Resnick
sp.p: Very good.
